```{r}
library(ggplot2)
a <- read.csv("../results/tables/annual_results.csv")
s <- read.csv("../results/independent_placebos/placebo_stats.csv")
plot_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size=19) + theme(legend.position="top",panel.grid.minor=element_blank())
```

## California’s tobacco control program

### A synthetic control replication

Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2010)

**Ying Zhang and Feng Yi Chew**  
STAT 5200 · Recorded presentation

Research question: How did Proposition 99 affect cigarette sales?

## Policy, data, and comparison group

- Proposition 99 passed in November 1988 and took effect in January 1989
- A 25-cent cigarette tax increase supported tobacco control and health programs
- Annual cigarette sales per capita, 1970–2000
- California plus 38 donor states
- Pretreatment: 1970–1988 · Post-treatment: 1989–2000

::: {.small}
Source: ADH (2010), Section 3.2. Sales are a proxy for consumption.
:::

## Constructing synthetic California

A weighted average of donor states approximates California before treatment.

$$\widehat{Y}_{CA,t}(0)=\sum_j w_jY_{j,t},\qquad w_j\geq0,\quad\sum_jw_j=1$$

- Match past sales and pretreatment predictors
- Choose predictor weights to improve pretreatment outcome fit
- Estimate the effect as actual minus synthetic sales after 1988

**Identification:** a stable counterfactual relationship, with no major spillovers or unaccounted California-specific shocks

::: {.small}
Source: ADH (2010), Sections 2–3. Fit supports the design but does not establish these assumptions.
:::

## Predictors and replication specification

| Predictor | Period |
|---|---|
| Log income, age 15–24 share, retail price | Average, 1980–1988 |
| Beer consumption | Average, 1984–1988 |
| Cigarette sales | 1975, 1980, 1988 separately |

Weight optimization: **1970–1988**

Implementation: `tidysynth` 0.2.1, bundled `smoking` data

::: {.small}
Source: ADH (2010), Table 1. Solver settings: margin 0.02, significance 7, bound 6.
:::

## The same five states dominate the synthetic control

| Donor state | Paper | Replication |
|---|---:|---:|
| Colorado | 16.4% | 14.88% |
| Connecticut | 6.9% | 6.17% |
| Montana | 19.9% | 20.88% |
| Nevada | 23.4% | 23.84% |
| Utah | 33.4% | 34.20% |

Weights sum to one and are nonnegative.

**Pretreatment RMSPE: 1.78 packs per capita**

::: {.small}
Source: ADH (2010), Table 2, and `results/tables/`. Displayed weights are rounded.
:::

## Actual sales diverge from synthetic California

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
trend <- rbind(data.frame(year=a$time_unit, sales=a$real_y, Series="California"),
               data.frame(year=a$time_unit, sales=a$synth_y, Series="Synthetic California"))
ggplot(trend, aes(year,sales,colour=Series,linetype=Series)) +
 geom_line(linewidth=1.1) + geom_vline(xintercept=1988,linetype="dotted") +
 scale_colour_manual(values=c("#182D40","#A32379")) +
 labs(x="Year",y="Packs per capita",colour=NULL,linetype=NULL) + plot_theme
```

::: {.small}
Source: corrected replication. Vertical line marks the last pretreatment year.
:::

## The estimated effects are close to the paper

| Quantity | Paper | Replication |
|---|---:|---:|
| Average reduction, 1989–2000 | Almost 20 packs | 18.85 packs |
| Percentage reduction | About 25% | 23.80% |
| Reduction in 2000 | About 26 packs | 25.58 packs |
| Pretreatment MSPE | About 3 | 3.17 |

**A close substantive replication, with numerical differences**

::: {.small}
Sources: ADH (2010), Section 3.3 and abstract; corrected replication. Our percentage divides the average reduction by mean synthetic sales. Packs are annual sales per capita.
:::

## California has the largest placebo ratio

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4
s <- s[order(s$mspe_ratio,decreasing=TRUE),]
s$Position <- seq_len(nrow(s))
ggplot(s,aes(Position,mspe_ratio,fill=type)) + geom_col(width=.8) +
 scale_fill_manual(values=c(Donor="#B5BEC5",Treated="#A32379")) +
 labs(x="States ranked by post/pre-MSPE ratio",y="Post/pre-MSPE ratio",fill=NULL) + plot_theme
```

Independent predictor optimization: California ranks **1 of 39**, rank p = **0.0256**.

::: {.small}
Source: `results/independent_placebos/`. Ratios measure squared divergence. The gap establishes the negative direction. This is a placebo comparison, not proof of random assignment.
:::

## Placebo fitting choices change the sensitivity analysis

| Pre-MSPE cutoff | Default donors | Independent donors | Independent rank p |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| No cutoff | 38 | 38 | 0.0256 |
| 20× California | 29 | 32 | 0.0303 |
| 5× California | 20 | 28 | 0.0345 |
| 2× California | 6 | 18 | 0.0526 |

California remains first. At the strictest cutoff, 19 total states give a minimum p-value of **1/19**.

::: {.small}
The default reuses California’s predictor weights. Independent fitting chooses them separately for each state. Published retained counts: 34, 29, 19. Sources: saved results; ADH (2010), Figures 5–7.
:::

## Lessons and implications for our project

- Check package conventions and solver arguments before interpreting results
- Rebuild diagnostics from the current model to avoid stale results
- Inspect placebo fit as well as California’s estimated effect
- Report numerical differences and sensitivity transparently

**Project application:** identify the counterfactual, justify the comparison group, and assess robustness

::: {.small}
Sales may differ from consumption through cross-border purchases or smuggling.
:::

```{r}

knitr::kable(b, digits=4)
```

Age share uses proportions. The donor-sample average is unweighted.
Log income has weaker balance and a small predictor weight.

Source: corrected replication; ADH (2010), Table 1.
